newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FOCUS-China fights local govt on oil smuggling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-China fights local govt on oil smuggling.

text.p: China has had some success at catching oil smugglers, but is being thwarted by local authorities turning a blind eye to the illicit trade, Chinese sources said on Wednesday.
Chinese officials said the central government is trying to clamp down on coastal authorities who are encouraging the smuggling to boost local economies and line local coffers.
Smuggling avoids paying import duties and taxes and can yield more than 500 yuan (US$60) per tonne on diesel -- the most common oil imported, traders said.
On a standard cargo of 30,000 tonnes, savings can amount to $1.8 million.
China makes most of the diesel it consumes. Last year it produced 44 million tonnes, while registered imports were 4.6 million tonnes.
Official data showed that diesel imports this year surged to 2.4 million tonnes in the first four months, a 77 percent jump from a year ago.
But state media said about one million tonnes of diesel had been smuggled into China so far this year. Oil traders said the figure could easily be higher.

"Authorities at all levels in the coastal regions must make breakthroughs in halting the smuggling of oil products and other key items as part of our anti-smuggling compaign in the second half of the year," Chinese vice-premier Li Langqing said at a national anti-smuggling meeting in Beijing on Tuesday, the People's Daily said.

The central government recently stationed "work teams" in coastal provinces, including Guangdong, Fujian and Zhejiang, to reinforce the smuggling crackdowns, said a source with Hainan Petrochemical Development Corp.
Li said some local governments allowed smuggling because of what he described as "local interests". But he said this caused "major damage in the state economy."
"Oil smuggling is not just an issue among individuals, like in the past," said a source with China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec), China's state refiner.
"Many coastal governments are involved. Cheap oil does help the economy. They have their concerns," said the source.
But while the smuggling crack down was to continue, officials said the Chinese authorities had already seen signs of success.
"In Hainan alone, we had two major crackdowns so far this year. We now don't see much smuggling here," the source said from the sourthern Chinese island.
During the crackdowns, authorities detained some cargoes from Singapore and confiscated the diesel, the source said.

"Based on reports we received recently, the smuggling situation has been improved largely," a source with China National Chemicals Import and Export Corp (Sinochem), a main state importer, said from Beijing.
A customs official at Fujian, a coastal province infamous for oil smuggling, said "intensive and strict" checks at customs had cut down smuggling in Fujian significantly in recent weeks.
"We are focusing on information collection, which makes it easier to cut down the smuggling," said the official.

After Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule, Beijing has closer links with the former British colony to trace oil flows and ship movements between the two sides, a well-placed source with one of China's state oil companies said.
Chinese traders have said they expected diesel imports to drop in the second half of the year in the face of rampant smuggling and high stockpiles at refineries in the first half.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3571)
